facts.a: Neapolitan pizza is the original: a soft, foldable disc with a puffy, blistered rim called the cornicione and a thin, almost wet center. It bakes in 60 to 90 seconds in a blazing hot oven, and the dough is nothing but flour, water, salt, and yeast - no oil, no sugar.
alt: The mother of all pizza. Soft and tender rather than crisp, with a leopard-spotted puffy rim, a delicate center, and a dough of only four ingredients: flour, water, salt, yeast. It goes into a roughly 450-degree-Celsius oven for barely a minute and a half.

A Neapolitan is soft, not crispy - people are always surprised by that. Puffy charred rim, thin tender middle, four-ingredient dough, and a bake so hot and fast the whole pizza is done in about 90 seconds.

Four ingredients, one minute, no compromise - that is Neapolitan in a sentence. Flour, water, salt and yeast make the dough, with no oil and no sugar, and a wood-fired oven around 450 degrees Celsius bakes it in 60 to 90 seconds. What comes out is soft and foldable, with a puffy, leopard-spotted cornicione and a thin, tender, almost wet center. It is not a synonym for thin crust in general; it is the specific style of Naples, and most pizza everywhere else descends from it.

alt: Ferociously hot: 430-480°C. The bake takes barely 90 seconds. That violent heat is what creates the leopard-spotted rim and keeps the center tender.
About 450 degrees Celsius, give or take. Sixty to ninety seconds and it's out. No home oven gets close, which is why home Neapolitan is always an approximation.

The number to remember is 450 degrees Celsius - the floor of a Neapolitan oven sits somewhere between 430 and 480, and the dome is hotter still. At that temperature a pizza needs only 60 to 90 seconds, which is exactly why 300 degrees is not 'plenty': a domestic oven tops out around 250 to 300 and can only ever produce an approximation. Nothing burns at that speed if the pizzaiolo keeps turning it; the heat is what blisters the rim and keeps the center tender.

facts.a: That soft, almost wet center is not a defect - it is the style. A true Neapolitan is tender and foldable, eaten with a knife and fork in Naples or folded 'a libretto' like a little book. If you want crisp, you want a Roman tonda, not a Neapolitan.
alt: It's supposed to be that way! The 90-second bake leaves the center delicate and moist. Neapolitans eat it with cutlery or folded in quarters. Crispness is the Roman virtue, not the Neapolitan one.

No, a soft center is not undercooked and it is not a mistake - it is the signature of the style. A Neapolitan spends only 60 to 90 seconds in a 450-degree oven, so the middle stays tender and moist while the rim puffs and blisters. Neapolitans eat it with a knife and fork or fold it 'a libretto', in quarters like a little book. If a pizzeria serves you one like that, they got it right. The crisp, crunchy disc some people expect is a Roman tonda.

Whoever told you a Neapolitan should snap like a cracker has confused Naples with Rome. Crispness belongs to the Roman tonda; the Neapolitan is meant to be soft and foldable, with a thin, almost wet center under the toppings and an airy cornicione around it. That texture comes straight from the fast, ferociously hot bake, and it is exactly what the STG specification describes. Bring cutlery or fold it - just do not call it soggy.

The dough usually contains a little olive oil, is rolled thinner than a Neapolitan, and bakes longer at a lower temperature - around 300 degrees Celsius for two to three minutes.
alt: The Roman round pizza is everything a Neapolitan is not: rolled thin, low rim, and baked until it audibly crunches - scrocchiarella means 'the little cruncher'. A touch of oil in the dough helps it crisp.
Thin and crisp edge to edge. Rome bakes lower and slower than Naples - about 300°C for a few minutes - and allows oil in the dough and even a rolling pin, which would be heresy in Naples.

Crisp is the whole point in Rome. The tonda is a round, thin pizza with barely any rim, rolled out - a rolling pin is perfectly acceptable here - from a dough that includes a little olive oil, then baked around 300 degrees Celsius for two to three minutes until it snaps. Cooler and slower than a Neapolitan oven, the opposite texture: dry, crunchy, edge to edge. It is more than a Neapolitan rolled thin - the oil, the pin and the bake all differ. Romans call it scrocchiarella.

Tray-baked, sold by weight, eaten standing up. Gabriele Bonci made this style famous in Rome with high-hydration, long-fermented doughs - airy inside, crisp underneath.

Think of al taglio as Rome's pizza counter rather than its pizza plate: big rectangular trays, cut with scissors to whatever size you point at, and charged by weight - typically per hundred grams. It is not a round pizza and it is not a heavy one. The modern dough runs very wet, 75 to 90 percent hydration, and cold-ferments for days, so the inside is open and airy like ciabatta while the base stays crisp. Gabriele Bonci is the name that made it famous.

Pinsa is the best food-marketing story of the century: invented around 2001, sold as ancient Rome. The flour blend (wheat, rice, soy) and high hydration make it genuinely lighter and crispier than most pizza, so I forgive the legend.

Let me be blunt: pinsa is not ancient, not a legionary's ration, and not older than pizza. It was invented around 2001 by Corrado Di Marco, a flour producer in Rome, and the 'ancient recipe' is a marketing story attached to it afterwards. What is real is the product: an oval flatbread from a wheat, rice and soy flour blend at very high hydration, crisp outside and airy inside, and genuinely lighter than most pizza. Enjoy it for what it is - a clever modern invention.

Alsace's thin crust has no yeast at all. No - focaccia is not a pizza base waiting for sauce, and it is not pizza without toppings. It is a bread in its own right, from Liguria: thick, dimpled with the fingertips, rich with olive oil both in the dough and pooled on top, and finished sparsely with salt, rosemary, maybe olives. Pizza is a topped dish whose base exists to carry the toppings; with focaccia the crumb itself is the point. Sauce it and you have made bad pizza on good bread.

People call focaccia 'thick pizza' all the time, and every time a Ligurian winces. It is not pizza. Focaccia is oil-rich, tall and dimpled, topped with little more than salt and rosemary, and it is eaten as bread. Pizza - the thin European kind I care about - is a base built to serve tomato, cheese and whatever else lands on it. Same oven, same flour, different purpose. The crumb is focaccia's star; the topping is pizza's.

No cheese, and that is the whole point. Sardenaira comes from around Sanremo in western Liguria: a soft, focaccia-like base, cooked tomato, anchovies, olives, capers and garlic. It's thin, but crisp-chewy rather than soft, and low-moisture mozzarella replaces fresh fior di latte.
alt: NY pizza is what happened when Neapolitan emigrants met gas ovens: oil and sugar in the dough for color and keeping quality, a 5-7 minute bake around 300°C, low-moisture mozzarella, and a slice you fold lengthwise. Great in its own right - just don't call it Neapolitan.

It is not Neapolitan, however Italian the grandparents were. New York style grew out of Neapolitan pizza when emigrants met gas deck ovens and American appetites: oil and sugar go into the dough, the bake stretches to 5-7 minutes around 300 degrees Celsius, and low-moisture mozzarella replaces fresh fior di latte. That makes a slice that is thin but sturdy and crisp-chewy - firm enough to fold lengthwise and eat walking - where a Neapolitan is soft, tender and eaten with a fork or folded on a plate.

Bigger is the least of the differences. People say New York pizza is just Neapolitan scaled up; it is not. The dough carries oil and sugar, which a Neapolitan dough never does, the oven is a gas deck at around 300 degrees rather than a wood fire at 450, the bake is 5-7 minutes instead of 90 seconds, and the cheese is low-moisture mozzarella. The result is crisp-chewy and foldable, not soft. A fine pizza on its own terms - just a different one.

Palermo's answer to pizza is closer to a bread. Sfincione is a thick, soft, spongy pan bake with cooked onion-tomato sauce, anchovies, hard caciocavallo and a crust of breadcrumbs on top. That is the whole idea of pizza al metro from Vico Equense near Naples: a long oval pizza, sized by length, split along its stretch into different toppings for different people. The dough is in the same family as Neapolitan pizza; only the shape changes, from round to long. Half a meter for a couple, a full meter for four or five, and the table shares.

One pizza, four quarters, one season each. Quattro stagioni keeps its toppings in separate quadrants: artichokes for spring, olives or basil for summer, mushrooms for autumn and prosciutto cotto for winter. Yes, the sections are the point. A quattro stagioni is divided into four quadrants that stand for the seasons - artichoke, olive or basil, mushroom, cooked ham - and the toppings are not mixed. facts.a: Thin crust keeps the ratio honest: every bite carries crust, sauce, and topping in balance, and the dough has to be good because it can't hide under volume. Thick styles have their place - but when the crust gets tall, the toppings become a casserole and the bread becomes filler. In Europe we settled this argument centuries ago.

More dough does not make a better pizza; it makes a bigger loaf. Thin crust keeps the ratio honest - crust, sauce and topping arrive together in every bite - and it exposes every flaw in the dough, because there is no volume to hide under. Once the crust grows tall, the toppings turn into a casserole and the bread into filler. Thick styles have their place, but Europe settled this argument centuries ago, and it settled it thin.

The 'more pizza' argument is exactly backwards. What you get with a thick crust is more bread, not more pizza - the tomato and cheese are diluted by a slab that mostly tastes of itself. Thin crust is the balanced version: every mouthful has base, sauce and topping in proportion, and the baker cannot hide a dull, underproofed dough beneath the height. Volume is not value here. Thin is not less food; it is the food, without the padding.

facts.a: Since 2010, 'Pizza Napoletana' has held STG status in the EU - Specialità Tradizionale Garantita, or Traditional Speciality Guaranteed. The rules pin down the dough ingredients, the hand-stretching, the wood-fired bake, and even the maximum diameter of 35 centimeters. It protects the recipe, not the region - anyone anywhere can make an STG-compliant Neapolitan if they follow the specification.
alt: It's an EU Traditional Speciality Guaranteed designation, held since 2010. STG stands for Specialità Tradizionale Garantita - Traditional Speciality Guaranteed - and Pizza Napoletana has carried it in the EU since 2010. It is not a geographic protection: the label guards the recipe, not the place, so a pizzeria in Berlin or Tokyo can produce an STG-compliant Neapolitan as long as it follows the specification to the letter. That specification is strict: four-ingredient dough, hand stretching only, a wood-fired oven, a 60-90 second bake, a maximum diameter of 35 centimeters and a cornicione of one to two centimeters.

Anywhere, by anyone, provided the rules are kept - that is the point of STG. Since 2010 Pizza Napoletana has been an EU Traditional Speciality Guaranteed, which protects a method rather than a territory; it is not a Naples-only badge. The method itself is spelled out: flour, water, salt and yeast, stretched by hand, baked in a wood-fired oven at around 485°C for 60 to 90 seconds, no wider than 35 cm, with a rim of one to two centimeters.

Founded in Naples in 1984, the Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana is a private association of pizza makers - not a government agency and not the EU body behind the STG label. What it does is certify pizzerias, anywhere in the world, that make vera pizza napoletana to its specification: four-ingredient dough, hand stretching, a wood-fired oven around 450 degrees and a 60-90 second bake. Look for the Pulcinella. That masked figure with a certificate number beside a pizzeria's entrance means the AVPN - the true Neapolitan pizza association, based in Naples since 1984 - has audited the place and found it compliant: the right dough, stretched by hand, baked in a wood oven at about 450 degrees for 60 to 90 seconds. They certify worldwide, so the logo means as much in Melbourne as in Naples. It is an association of pizzaioli, not a state authority.

facts.a: The cornicione is the raised rim of a Neapolitan pizza - the 'frame' of the picture. A good cornicione is airy like fresh bread inside, leopard-spotted outside, never doughy or dense.
alt: The rim. In Naples it should be one to two centimeters, blistered and light as brioche inside. Stretching pushes all the fermentation gas to the edge; the oven does the rest. Dense cornicione means underproofed dough - the tell of a rushed pizzeria.

Cornicione is the Italian for the raised rim of a Neapolitan pizza - the picture frame around the toppings. It puffs on purpose: while stretching, the pizzaiolo presses the fermentation gas from the center out to the edge, and the 450-degree oven inflates that ring in seconds. A good one is one to two centimeters tall, leopard-spotted outside and as airy as fresh bread inside. Dense and chewy is not a virtue; it is the mark of underproofed dough.

Far from leftover crust, the cornicione is where a Neapolitan shows its quality. The rim rises because stretching drives all the gas outward from the center and the ferocious oven bakes it before it can escape - one to two centimeters of blistered, brioche-light air. Inside it should be open and tender; outside, charred spots. If it comes out heavy and doughy, the dough was underproofed or rushed. In Naples the rim is not discarded; it is the point.

facts.a: Two different pizzas, both Roman. Tonda is the round one: a thin, crisp, rolled-out disc with almost no rim, baked around 300 degrees Celsius for two to three minutes, ordered whole at a sit-down pizzeria - the scrocchiarella. Al taglio is the tray one: a rectangular pan pizza from a very wet dough of 75 to 90 percent hydration, airy inside, crisp underneath, cut with scissors and sold by weight at a counter. Round and crisp is tonda; rectangular and by the hundred grams is al taglio.
alt: No - al taglio is not the round crispy one, and tonda is not the tray. Tonda (round) is the thin, cracker-crisp disc you order whole in a Roman pizzeria, rolled thin and baked at about 300°C for a few minutes. Al taglio (by the cut) is the rectangular tray pizza sold by weight from a counter, scissored into pieces, made from a high-hydration dough that bakes into an open, ciabatta-like crumb on a crisp base. Shape, dough and how you buy it all differ.

Shape first: round is tonda, rectangular is al taglio. Then the dough: tonda is a firmer dough with a little oil, rolled thin and baked crisp edge to edge; al taglio is a wet 75-90 percent hydration dough, cold-fermented for days, that bakes into something airy and open with a crunchy bottom. Then the purchase: a tonda is a whole pizza at a sit-down place, al taglio is cut with scissors and priced by weight. People who call the tray pizza 'tonda' have simply got the two swapped.

They share a city and nothing else that matters. Anyone who tells you al taglio is just a tonda cut into slices has it wrong: the tonda is a round, thin, crisp disc - the scrocchiarella - baked whole for one person, while al taglio is a rectangular tray pizza from a very wet, long-fermented dough, airy inside, crisp underneath, cut to order with scissors and charged by weight. Different dough, different shape, different counter. Sit down for a tonda; stand up for al taglio.

facts.a: Naples is soft, Rome is crisp - that is the headline. A Neapolitan bakes at 430 to 480 degrees Celsius for 60 to 90 seconds from a dough of only flour, water, salt and yeast, stretched by hand and never rolled: puffy leopard-spotted cornicione, thin tender center, eaten with a fork or folded. A Roman tonda bakes around 300 degrees for two to three minutes from a dough with a little olive oil, rolled out thin with a pin, low rim, crunchy edge to edge - the scrocchiarella.
alt: Not the same pizza, not even close. People who say Naples and Rome make basically the same thing are ignoring five differences. Temperature: Naples 430-480°C, Rome about 300°C. Time: 60-90 seconds against two to three minutes. Texture: Neapolitan soft and foldable with a puffed rim; Roman tonda thin and crisp with almost no rim. Oil: none in a Neapolitan dough, a little in a Roman one. Rolling pin: forbidden in Naples, routine in Rome. Two cities, two philosophies of dough.

Backwards - Neapolitan is the soft one, Roman is the crunchy one, never the other way round. The Neapolitan gets its tenderness from a violent 60-90 second bake at around 450 degrees and a four-ingredient dough opened by hand; the rim balloons, the middle stays almost wet. The Roman tonda goes the opposite way: dough with a touch of oil, flattened thin with a rolling pin, baked cooler at about 300°C for a few minutes until it snaps. Soft versus crisp is the whole distinction.

A dial from tender to crunchy. At the Naples end: no oil, no rolling pin, hand-stretched dough, an oven at 430-480 degrees Celsius, a 60 to 90 second bake, and a pizza that is soft, blistered at the rim and delicate in the center. At the Rome end: a little oil in the dough, a rolling pin, around 300 degrees for two to three minutes, and a thin, crisp scrocchiarella with barely a rim. A Roman is not a thinner Neapolitan; it is a different dough baked a different way.
